title: Unified Pension Scheme and the old pension debate
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Old pension, NPS and the Unified Pension Scheme approved in August 2024: what each offers, the positions taken and the questions that remain.
body:
Few subjects stir government employees as much as the pension they will receive after thirty years of service. It is a promise made at the start of a career and tested at its end. Over the last two decades India has moved from one pension design to another, and the Unified Pension Scheme announced in 2024 is the most recent attempt to settle the argument. This post explains the three schemes in plain terms, sets out what the Cabinet approved, and describes the questions that remain.

## The old pension scheme

For government employees recruited before 2004, the pension was a **defined benefit**: a formula based on years of service and the last pay drawn decided the amount, and the Government paid it from its own budget. Employees did not contribute towards it during service. The security was complete: the retiree knew in advance roughly what he or she would receive each month, and the amount rose with dearness relief.

## The National Pension System

The Government's view, formed after the review of old-age income security begun in 1999, was that unfunded pension promises would become a growing burden on future budgets. A Finance Ministry notification dated 22 December 2003 made the **National Pension System (NPS)** mandatory for new central government recruits from **1 January 2004**, excluding the armed forces. Many States followed for their own employees. The NPS is a **defined contribution** scheme: the employee and the employer put money into an individual account, the money is invested through regulated pension fund managers, and the final corpus depends on contributions and market returns. On retirement, part of the corpus must be used to buy an annuity which provides the monthly income. The scheme is regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, which became a statutory authority in 2014. In 2009 the NPS was opened to all citizens on a voluntary basis.

The difficulty, from the employee's side, is uncertainty. Two employees with identical careers could retire with very different pensions depending on when markets rose or fell, and no one could tell in advance what the monthly income would be. Employee organisations and Opposition parties have protested against the NPS for this reason, objecting also to the deduction from salary, and have demanded a return to the old scheme. Several States, including Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh, told the Centre that they would revert to the old scheme for their employees.

## The 2024 decision

In March 2023 the Government set up a committee headed by the former Finance Secretary T. V. Somanathan to look at ways of improving the NPS for government employees. On **24 August 2024** the Union Cabinet approved the **Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)**. It offers an **assured pension** while keeping a funded structure. The features announced were:

- **Assured pension:** 50 percent of the average basic pay drawn over the last twelve months before superannuation, for a minimum qualifying service of 25 years. For shorter service, down to a minimum of ten years, the amount is proportionate.
- **Assured family pension:** 60 percent of the employee's pension immediately before death.
- **Assured minimum pension:** ₹10,000 per month on superannuation after at least ten years of service.
- **Inflation indexation:** the assured pension, family pension and minimum pension are to receive dearness relief based on the All India Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers, in the same way as for serving employees.
- **Lump sum at superannuation:** in addition to gratuity, one-tenth of monthly emoluments (pay plus dearness allowance) for every completed six months of service. The announcement said that this payment would not reduce the assured pension.
- **Contributions:** the employee's contribution stays at 10 percent of basic pay plus dearness allowance, while the Government's contribution rises from 14 to 18.5 percent.
- **Choice:** employees in the NPS could choose between the NPS and the UPS, and the choice, once made, was to be final. The scheme was to begin from 1 April of the following financial year, and the Government said it would benefit about **23 lakh** central government employees. State governments were also free to adopt it; the Centre noted that over nine million State employees are in the NPS.
- **Fiscal cost:** reports of the announcement quoted about ₹800 crore as the one-time cost of arrears and about ₹6,250 crore as the additional annual cost in the first year.

## The positions

The debate that followed was predictable and, in a sense, healthy.

- **Many employee organisations** continue to seek restoration of the **old pension scheme**, arguing that an employee who has served the State for decades should not have the old age income linked to the stock market. For them, any scheme in which the employee contributes towards the pension is a departure from the original promise.
- **Others** regard the UPS as a step forward because it brings assurance of a minimum level of income, indexation and family pension, while seeking improvements, for example in the treatment of employees with shorter service, and in the one-time nature of the choice.
- **The Government's view**, expressed in the Somanathan Committee's exercise, was that a return to the old system was not fiscally sustainable, and that the UPS offers a balance between assurance for the employee and a funded structure that does not leave an uncertain liability for the future. Reports of the Cabinet decision said that the Prime Minister described the scheme as one which ensures dignity and financial security for government employees, while some Opposition leaders criticised the announcement.

## Questions that remain

Any pension design raises questions, and it is useful to list the ones employees ask most often:

1. **Is the choice reversible?** The announcement said the choice would be final once exercised, so employees need clear information about how their own service profile compares under each option.
2. **What about those who have already retired under the NPS?** The announcement said the provisions would extend to past NPS retirees with arrears, but arrears were to be paid at PPF interest rates.
3. **What about employees of States?** The UPS is designed for adoption by State governments, but each State must decide for itself, so the position of the nine million State employees varies.
4. **How are shorter careers treated?** The 25-year threshold for a full assured pension matters for those who enter service later in life.
5. **What of pensioners outside the Government?** Millions of private-sector and unorganised workers have no assured pension at all, and for them the debate is academic. The minimum pension under the EPS-95 scheme, which BMS has asked to be raised from ₹1,000 to ₹7,500 in its February 2026 charter of demands, is a case in point.

## BMS and pensions

BMS federations of government employees have taken part in consultations on pensions. Their emphasis has been on an **assured pension** for every worker who has served, on the protection of those who joined after 2004, and on fair treatment for State employees. More widely, the national conference at Puri in February 2026 asked that a new labour policy guarantee living wages and comprehensive social security to every worker. In BMS's view, the question of pensions should not be confined to the permanent employees of the Government: the vast number of workers in private industry, in contract jobs and in the unorganised sector need an assured old-age income too.

## The principle

A pension is a promise to a person who has served. Systems can be designed in different ways, and a nation has the right to ask what it can afford. But whatever the method, the assurance must not be lost. A scheme should be judged by a simple test: can a retired employee, in the fifteenth year of retirement, still meet the cost of food, medicine and a roof?
